Official Week 9 Objectives

1. Distinguish S. epidermidis, S. saprophyticus, S. pyogenes, S. agalactiae, S. pneumoniae, Enterococcus spp., and viridans streptococci based on laboratory characteristics.
2. List the virulence factors and major diseases associated with S. aureus, S. saprophyticus, S. epidermidis, S. pyogenes, S. agalactiae, and S. pneumoniae.
3. Describe the pathogenesis of toxic shock syndrome, scarlet fever, puerperal sepsis, and dental caries.

How to think through this lecture
Start with catalase. If Staph, go to coagulase and mannitol. If Strep/Enterococcus, go to hemolysis, then use the one defining lab test that separates the organisms in that branch.
Slides 2–5The first branch: Staph vs Strep/EnterococcusLO 1

Three medically important genera

  • Staphylococcus: skin colonizer, person-to-person spread, catalase positive, may be α/β/γ hemolytic; some species ferment mannitol.
  • Streptococcus and Enterococcus: catalase negative branch.
  • The catalase reaction converts H2O2 → H2O + O2; visible oxygen bubbling marks a positive test.
Do not miss
Staphylococcus = catalase positive. Streptococcus/Enterococcus = catalase negative. This is the highest-level split on the deck's final identification tree.
Legacy-note enrichment
The older course note spells out the coagulase test mechanism: coagulase converts fibrinogen to fibrin. It also explicitly states that S. aureus is coagulase positive, while S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are coagulase negative.
Slides 5–14Staphylococcus: identify S. aureus, then know what makes it dangerousLO 1–2

S. aureus — deck ID

  • Coagulase positive.
  • Ferments mannitol; deck shows the medium turning yellow.
  • Skin infections include furuncle and cellulitis; the deck notes “50% MRSA.”

Coagulase-negative Staph — deck emphasis

  • S. epidermidis: most frequent CoNS in clinical disease; nosocomial infection + biofilm; prosthetic devices; normal skin flora and frequent blood-culture contaminant; bacteremia in neutropenic patients.
  • S. saprophyticus: lower UTIs in young women; deck labels it the second most common cause.
  • Deck also names S. lugdunensis, S. capitis, and S. haemolyticus.

Exfoliative toxin → SSSS

The deck says exfoliative toxins are produced by ~5% of strains and digest an adhesive protein, decreasing keratinocyte adhesion so epithelium detaches and sheds.

TSST-1 → toxic shock

The deck presents TSST-1 as a superantigen syndrome with very large IL-2 release, menstrual and non-menstrual disease, and multi-organ failure.

Leukocidins

The current deck visually depicts both extracellular and intracellular S. aureus interacting with leukocytes and leukocidin-mediated injury.

Enterotoxins

The current deck names enterotoxins and shows food-associated imagery, but does not spell out timing or symptom details in text.

Legacy-note enrichment
Useful add-ons not explicitly named in the current slide text: exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1; TSST-1 cross-links MHC II to the T-cell receptor; enterotoxin is preformed and causes rapid food poisoning; novobiocin classically separates S. epidermidis (sensitive) from S. saprophyticus (resistant). Keep these as enrichment, not a replacement for the deck.
Lab trap
The current deck's final tree explicitly contrasts S. aureus (hemolytic, mannitol positive, yellow) with S. epidermidis (non-hemolytic, mannitol negative, white). It does not place novobiocin on that final tree.
Slides 15–29Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep)LO 1–3

Strep morphology and classification

  • Streptococci are non-motile facultative anaerobes that divide in one plane and remain in end-to-end chains.
  • Blood agar hemolysis is a major branch point; β-hemolytic streptococci can be serologically classified by Lancefield antigens.
  • S. pyogenes = Group A Strep; the deck shows presumptive bacitracin sensitivity as a zone with no growth around a Group A disk.
GAS factor / featureCurrent deck emphasis

Hyaluronic acid capsuleSame structure as human hyaluronic acid → camouflage; binds skin and pharyngeal epithelium
Lipoteichoic acid + F proteinBind fibronectin for adherence
StreptokinaseClot lysis → dissemination
Streptolysin O & SPore formation in human cells → tissue invasion
Hyaluronidase / RNase / DNaseTissue spread
Suppurative disease on the deck
Erysipelas · pharyngitis · lymphangitis · cellulitis.
Scarlet fever pathogenesis
The deck ties scarlet fever to streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (Spe), with strawberry tongue, a blanching finely papular rash, and Pastia's lines. The following slide presents superantigen binding of MHC II + T-cell receptor with marked IL-2 release.

Post-streptococcal immune disease

  • Glomerulonephritis: deck shows hump-like subepithelial deposits of nephritogenic antigens and immune complexes.
  • Rheumatic fever: deck states TH1 cells damage heart valves and shows verrucae.
  • Sydenham chorea / PANDAS: the deck includes a dedicated follow-up slide with movement/neuropsychiatric associations.
Legacy-note enrichment
The older note frames acute rheumatic fever as a post-pharyngitis immune cross-reaction and PSGN as immune-complex disease after pharyngeal or skin infection. Those timing/mechanism details are not all stated on the current deck, so treat them as secondary enrichment.
Slides 30–33Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep)LO 1–3

Identity

  • Lancefield Group B.
  • Encapsulated; weakly β- or α-hemolytic.
  • Colonizes GI/GU tract of up to 35% of pregnant women.
  • Deck states 50–75% transmission to babies at birth.

Disease

  • Puerperal sepsis / childbed fever.
  • Neonatal sepsis: bacteremia, meningitis, pneumonia.
  • Also affects compromised hosts; deck notes two-thirds are healthy.
Pathogenesis connection
Deck slide 32 links degradative enzymes, especially hyaluronidase, to tissue spread from mother to baby; hemolytic pigment is shown with resistance to phagocyte elimination and placental penetration.
Legacy-note enrichment
The older note adds standard prevention language: prenatal screening with intrapartum penicillin/ampicillin for carriers. This prevention detail is not stated on the current deck pages provided.
Slides 34–36Viridans streptococci: oral flora, caries, and endocarditisLO 1–3
  • Viridans streptococci are non-typable by the Lancefield method and normal flora of the mouth/pharynx.
  • The deck shows α-hemolysis and no exotoxins on the viridans plate.
  • Dental caries: sugar-driven microbial growth → localized acidification → demineralization.
  • Mutans streptococci include S. mutans and S. sobrinus; sucrose is converted to acetic and lactic acid.
  • Deck associates viridans streptococci with infective endocarditis (50%).
Dental caries pathogenesis
Sucrose → mutans streptococcal growth/metabolism → acetic + lactic acid → localized acidification → tooth demineralization.
Legacy-note enrichment
The older note adds that viridans streptococci are optochin resistant and bile insoluble and can produce dextrans from sucrose to support adherence. The current deck's final tree uses optochin to identify pneumococcus but does not explicitly spell out both viridans comparison points in text.
Slides 37–41Streptococcus pneumoniaeLO 1–2
  • Deck imagery connects pneumococcus to pneumonia, otitis media, sinus disease, and meningitis.
  • Growth: small translucent colonies; mucoid = capsule; α-hemolytic.
  • Optochin susceptible (ethylhydrocuprine HCl) with a zone of inhibition, in contrast to the viridans plate shown beside it.
  • Epidemiology: asymptomatic carriage; deck lists ~15% in school-age children and ~5% in supervising adults.
Current-deck pneumococcal factorFunction shown
PneumolysinReleased from lysed organisms; binds cholesterol → pores and decreased ciliary motility
IgA proteaseNamed on deck
HyaluronidaseExtracellular matrix tissue spread
NeuraminidaseSialic acid cleavage → increased spread
Legacy-note enrichment
The older note explicitly identifies the polysaccharide capsule as the most important virulence factor and summarizes classic disease associations (meningitis, otitis, pneumonia, sinusitis). It also adds bile solubility and vaccine details. Use these as enrichment; the current deck itself emphasizes mucoid capsule morphology, optochin, epidemiology, and the enzyme panel.
Slides 42–43Enterococcus: bile-esculin positive and salt tolerantLO 1
  • Residence: GI, GU, and biliary tracts; deck names E. faecalis and E. faecium.
  • Deck lists γ-hemolysis.
  • Bile-esculin: Enterococcus and Group D strep hydrolyze esculin to esculetin; esculetin reacts with ferric ions and turns the agar black.
  • 6.5% NaCl: the deck uses growth in 6.5% NaCl to identify Enterococcus and distinguish it from S. gallolyticus.
Legacy-note enrichment
The older note adds clinical context: enterococci are major nosocomial pathogens causing UTIs, biliary infections, and endocarditis, with important antibiotic resistance including VRE.
Slide 44Master Gram-positive cocci identification treeLO 1
BranchDeck rule
Catalase +Staphylococcus (pairs/clusters)
Coagulase +S. aureus: hemolytic, mannitol +, yellow
Coagulase −S. epidermidis: non-hemolytic, mannitol −, white
Catalase − → α hemolysisOptochin susceptible + bile soluble → S. pneumoniae
Catalase − → β hemolysisBacitracin + → S. pyogenes; hippurate + CAMP + → S. agalactiae
Catalase − → γ hemolysisBile-esculin + and 6.5% NaCl + → Enterococcus; bile-esculin + and 6.5% NaCl − → non-Enterococcus
One-line exam map
Catalase → coagulase if Staph; hemolysis if Strep. Then bacitracin/CAMP for β, optochin for α, and bile-esculin + 6.5% NaCl for γ.

Five checks before you leave

  1. Can you build the entire slide-44 ID tree from memory?
  2. Can you pair Protein A, M protein, CAMP factor, pneumolysin, and bile-esculin with the correct organism?
  3. Can you explain toxic shock syndrome, scarlet fever, puerperal sepsis, and dental caries mechanistically?
  4. Can you distinguish S. epidermidis from S. saprophyticus using the deck plus the explicitly labeled legacy enrichment?
  5. Can you separate pneumococcus, viridans, GAS, GBS, and Enterococcus using a single defining lab test?
